A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SMILING research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original continuous-control experiments with state-only and state-action demonstrations, plus a linear-function ablation in Section 6.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds DiffAIL comparisons and an expert-demonstration-size study in Section 6 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains expert score pretraining, score matching on aggregated learner states, and RL updates using the same difference-of-losses cost. The state-action adaptation also already appears in v1; no proposed algorithm or architecture change is established.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six tasks from DeepMind Control Suite and HumanoidBench, using both state-only and state-action demonstrations. The new demonstration-size sweep changes sample quantities within Humanoid Walk, not task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds DiffAIL to the state-only and state-action comparisons in Figures 2 and 4. Results are plotted for Ball in Cup Catch and Cheetah Run; numerical failures are reported for the four humanoid tasks. DAC, IQ-Learn, and BC remain.

E3.justification: Appendix D.2 introduces a Humanoid Walk sweep over 1K, 2K, 5K, 10K, 25K, and 125K expert states, evaluated after 3M training steps; Figure 5 averages the last 100 training epochs. The BC description also changes from maximum average episode reward to maximum episode reward, without establishing whether its underlying evaluation changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted sensitivity study testing expert-data efficiency against DAC on Humanoid Walk, with final-performance and learning-curve evidence in Figures 5–6. The existing linear-function ablation and humanoid visual case study are retained after relocation.

E5.justification: The corresponding benchmark curves retain five-random-seed reporting and shaded variability. The new demonstration-size results also use five seeds. No increase in repeated-run counts, new uncertainty-reporting practice, or significance-testing procedure is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds DiffAIL outcomes and demonstration-size results showing SMILING near expert performance with 5K states while DAC reaches similar performance with 25K. Appendix D.5 newly reports absolute expert returns. Existing comparator curves and the linear ablation are retained; Figures 8–9 redisplay results on unnormalized axes rather than establish performance changes.

T1.justification: The DS-divergence definition, assumptions, Theorem 1, supporting lemmas, and mathematical proofs remain substantively unchanged. The discriminator-expressiveness comparison moves from Section 5.1 to Appendix A. Equation renumbering and the changed attribution of Lemma 1 do not alter its mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: score-matching-based imitation, first- and second-order bounds without compounding errors, and strong continuous-control performance without expert actions. The additional experiments support these retained claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 removes Section 4's caveat that optimizing a strong divergence can be needlessly complex when relevant reward features can be specified in advance. It adds a tentative explanation linking DiffAIL's numerical failures to high-dimensional humanoid features and interprets the demonstration-size study as evidence of more efficient expert-data use.

D1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds the expert-training plateau criterion and task-specific training budgets, plus DiffAIL implementation and network-size information. These expand documentation without establishing changed expert-training procedures. The SMILING/DAC hyperparameter table and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands discussion to additional work including f-IRL, LS-IQ, primal Wasserstein imitation, energy-based score matching, dual approaches, and diffusion-reward methods. These broaden coverage within the existing research positioning. Numerous other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: the discriminator comparison moves to Appendix A, while state-action experiments and the expressiveness ablation move into an expanded Appendix D with short main-text summaries. Preliminaries and experimental prose are condensed, appendix organization changes, and acknowledgments are added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially rearranges the visual presentation, moving the humanoid montage, state-action curves, linear ablation, and environment table into the appendices. It adds demonstration-size Figures 5–6 and unnormalized-return Figures 8–9, and expands comparison plots and legends with DiffAIL. The unnormalized panels redisplay existing results.

improvement.justification: The demonstration-size study and DiffAIL evaluation strengthen the empirical support, while expert-training details and absolute-return reporting improve reproducibility and interpretation. These gains remain limited to existing tasks, and DiffAIL comparisons are incomplete on humanoids because of reported numerical failures. Removing the useful IPM applicability caveat weakens balance, but the added evidence and documentation provide a limited net improvement.
